title: Psalm 89: Where Is Your Loving Devotion of Old?
summary: The psalm begins by singing of God's loving devotion and faithfulness, praising him as the incomparable ruler of heaven and sea, and rehearsing at length his sworn covenant with David: an everlasting dynasty and a throne as enduring as the sun and moon. Then it turns sharply. God has rejected his anointed king, broken down his walls, and cast his throne to the ground, and the psalmist asks how long this will last and where God's promised love has gone. Book III of the Psalms closes with a brief blessing of the LORD.
story: Psalm 89 is the climax and the end of Book III (Psalms 73 to 89). The Psalter's first two books were framed by God's promise to David: Psalm 2 announced his anointed king on Zion, and Psalm 72, closing Book II, prayed for a king whose reign would bless all nations. Book III has been darkening since Psalm 73, and here the darkness reaches the throne itself. The covenant God swore to David in 2 Samuel 7 seems to have failed: the king is humiliated and the city in ruins. Many readers see the fourth book of the Psalms (Psalms 90 to 106) as the answer to this crisis. It opens with the only psalm attributed to Moses and proclaims again and again that the LORD reigns, directing Israel's hope back to God's own kingship while the promise to David waits. The Bible's larger story carries the question of Psalm 89 forward to the coming of a son of David.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to Ethan the Ezrahite. Chronicles names an Ethan among the chief Levite singers appointed under David (1 Chronicles 15:17, 19), and 1 Kings 4:31 lists an Ethan the Ezrahite among the wise men whom Solomon surpassed. As with the headings generally, scholars debate whether this is authorship, a guild attribution, or a later editorial note, and whether these Ethans are the same person.

The lament of verses 38 to 51 describes a Davidic king rejected, his crown in the dust, his walls broken and his strongholds in ruins, and his youth cut short. Many interpreters connect this with the Babylonian conquest of Jerusalem: in 597 BC the eighteen-year-old king Jehoiachin was carried off to Babylon (2 Kings 24:8-15), and in 587 or 586 BC the city and temple were destroyed and the dynasty lost its throne. Others propose an earlier crisis that humiliated a Davidic king without ending the line, such as the Egyptian invasion under Shishak in the reign of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25-26) or the death of Josiah in battle in 609 BC. Some scholars also think the hymn of verses 1 to 37 is older and was later joined to the lament. The psalm itself names no king.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern kings made treaties with vassal rulers, often sealed with oaths, and a royal grant could promise a dynasty to a loyal servant and his heirs. God's covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:8-16) resembles such a grant: it promises David a lasting house and throne, and it provides for discipline of disobedient sons without revoking the promise. Psalm 89 quotes and expands that promise in verses 19 to 37, including the rod and stripes of verse 32, which echo 2 Samuel 7:14.

The opening hymn draws on imagery a first reader would recognize. Neighboring peoples told of a storm god defeating the sea or a sea monster to win kingship among the gods. The psalm assigns those victories to the LORD: he rules the raging sea and crushed Rahab, a chaos monster whose name also served as a nickname for Egypt (verse 10). Tabor and Hermon, two prominent mountains in the north of Israel, join the praise. The assembly and council of the holy ones in verses 5 to 7 is the heavenly court around God's throne, in which no being compares with him. The horn (verses 17 and 24) was a common symbol of strength, taken from the image of a wild ox.
literary: Psalm 89 is a royal psalm that combines three kinds of material: a hymn to God's power and faithfulness (verses 1 to 18), an oracle recounting God's covenant with David (verses 19 to 37), and a lament over its apparent failure (verses 38 to 51). The doxology in verse 52 closes Book III, as similar blessings close each of the Psalter's first four books (Psalms 41:13; 72:18-19; 106:48). The two key words are loving devotion and faithfulness, each used seven times. The first half builds up these words to the heavens; the second half throws them back at God. Words from the promise are deliberately reversed in the lament: God said he would exalt the king's horn and crush his foes, and now he has exalted the right hand of his foes; he promised never to violate his covenant, and now he has renounced it. Placing the full promise before the lament makes the complaint as sharp as possible, because the psalmist is holding God to God's own words.

outline.t: Singing of God's love and his oath to David
The incomparable God who rules heaven, sea, and earth
The covenant with David: chosen, anointed, and made firstborn
Discipline for sons, but a promise that cannot be broken
The lament: the anointed rejected and the throne cast down
How long? Remember your servant's reproach

doctrines.note: The psalm is built on the covenant God swore to David, a promise that sons would be disciplined for disobedience but the dynasty would never be abandoned. Its lament is possible only because God bound himself by oath.

The anointed king of verses 20 and 38 is God's chosen son and firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. When the historical kings failed, this language became the foundation of Israel's hope for a coming Messiah.
Loving devotion and faithfulness are the psalm's key words. They define God's character, and the psalm appeals to them even when events seem to deny them.
The psalm shows faith that argues with God on the basis of his promises. It does not resolve the contradiction between promise and experience; it brings it before God and still ends in blessing.

words.note: Chesed, loving devotion. It names God's loyal, covenant-keeping love. It appears seven times, first as the theme of the song (verse 1), then as a promise to David (verses 24, 28, and 33), and finally as a question: “Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old?” (verse 49).

Emunah, faithfulness. From the root meaning firm or reliable (the same root as amen, which closes the psalm), it describes God's steadiness in keeping his word. Like chesed, it appears seven times, and the lament tests whether it holds.

Berit, covenant. The word describes a binding relationship established by oath, with promises and obligations. God's covenant with David is mentioned in verses 3, 28, 34, and 39, and the last of these accuses God of having renounced it.

Mashiach, anointed one. The king was anointed with oil as a sign of God's choice (verse 20). The Greek translation is christos. Verses 38 and 51 speak of God's anointed rejected and mocked, a phrase that becomes weighty in light of the New Testament.

christ: Psalm 89 is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of the promise that runs from David to Jesus, and of the crisis that promise faced. Paul's sermon in Acts 13:22 echoes verse 20 (“I have found David”) in tracing the line of David to Jesus. The book of Revelation describes Jesus in the psalm's language as “the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1:5), drawing together verse 27 (firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth) and verse 37 (a faithful witness in the sky). The psalm's lament finds its deepest echo in the Gospels: the anointed one is rejected, his crown is mocked, and his enemies taunt him, exactly the reproach of verse 51. The New Testament's answer to the psalm's question is not that God forgot his oath but that he kept it in a way no one expected, by raising David's son from the dead and giving him a throne that will not end (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:29-36).

hard.q: Did God break his promise to David?
hard.a:
The psalm itself raises this question as sharply as possible. God swore that David's throne would endure like the sun and moon (verses 36 and 37), yet the psalmist sees the king humiliated and the throne thrown down. The difficulty is real: after the exile, no descendant of David ruled as king in Jerusalem again.

Several responses are given. First, the covenant itself foresaw discipline: 2 Samuel 7:14 and Psalm 89:30-32 warn that disobedient sons would be punished, so the fall of the kings was not outside the promise's terms. Second, the promise concerned the line of David, not every king in it, and the line survived exile; Jehoiachin was later released and honored in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27-30), and the genealogies of Matthew and Luke trace Jesus through David's descendants. Third, Christians hold that the promise was fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David raised to an everlasting throne. Jewish interpreters have understood the promise as awaiting fulfillment in a Messiah still to come. Readers who take any of these views agree with the psalmist on one thing: the answer must come from God keeping his word, and the psalm is right to ask him to keep it.

questions: The psalmist holds God to his own promises. Is there a promise of God you have struggled to reconcile with what you see?
The psalm places a long hymn of praise before its lament. How might remembering God's character shape the way you complain to him?
Book III ends with “Blessed be the LORD forever” immediately after a bitter lament. What does it mean to bless God when the question has not been answered?
